generalizedRange: Northern Australia's rivers and coasts; scattered tropical populations elsewhere
hook: It once swam the coasts of 75 countries. Its saw snags every net.

story.text: The largetooth sawfish is a shark-like ray of up to seven metres, a quarter of it toothed saw.
The saw is a sense organ first: it reads the faint electric fields of prey, then swings sideways to stun them.
Pups push upstream for their first years — in the Fitzroy River, more than 400 km from the sea.
It once lived in the coastal waters of 75 countries, the widest range of any sawfish.
The saw snags in gillnets and trawls, and outside Australia a caught sawfish is usually kept for its fins and rostrum.
Since 1900 its range has shrunk by an estimated 61 percent, mapped by researchers from Simon Fraser and Charles Darwin universities.
Northern Australia is now the Indo-West Pacific stronghold: protected in all its waters since 2000, still common in the Fitzroy.
Surveys keep the count: Murdoch University with the Nyikina-Mangala Rangers tracked 32 juveniles in the Fitzroy over eight years, and CSIRO with the APN Rangers found 47 on the Archer River in 2022.
Trade has been banned under CITES since 2007, and the Sawfish Conservation Society asks anyone who meets a sawfish, or finds an old saw, to report it.
To witness the largetooth sawfish is to keep faith with tropical rivers, and the floods that carry each year's pups upstream.

reproduction.text: Litters of one to thirteen pups, each about 75 cm long, arrive after a five-month gestation and only every other year — and a female is not mature until roughly ten years old.

insight.text: In Australia this ray counts as the largest freshwater fish — juveniles have been recorded more than 400 km up the Fitzroy River before they ever reach the sea.
